cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica) plantation leaf, mostly factory blends
processing: Ripe pu-erh fermented and pressed a decade or more ago and left to rest: the pile smell disappears, the residual roughness oxidises away and, in humid storage, the tea picks up a soft aged aroma that the trade calls chen xiang.
harvest_season: Irrelevant now; the tea is sold by production year, factory and storage.
appearance_dry: A loosened, dull dark-brown cake or brick, buds faded to a muted gold, smelling of old wood and dried fruit rather than earth.
appearance_liquor: Deep, clear, glossy red-brown to mahogany.
appearance_wet: Soft, dark, fully relaxed leaves with a clean, sweet, slightly camphorous smell.
taste_profile: Smooth, quiet and sweet: dates, old wood, a creamy rice-soup texture, light camphor and a herbal, ginseng-like note from humid storage, no earthiness or pile smell, and a long gentle finish.

brewing.notes: Rinse twice with boiling water and let the leaf rest a minute. Boiling water, a clay pot and patience; old ripe tea gives long, even sessions and the late steeps can be simmered.

vintage_note: Aged shu means ten or more years from pressing, and the market is mostly factory tea from roughly 1995–2012 (Menghai 7572 and 8592, Kunming 7581 bricks, Xiaguan ripe tuo) plus Hong Kong-stored loose ripe from restaurant stocks; genuinely old ripe from the 1980s exists but is rare and expensive, though still far cheaper than aged sheng of the same era. The change with age is gentler than in sheng: the pile smell goes, the texture softens and a camphor-and-herb aroma arrives in humid storage, while Kunming-dry tea just gets cleaner and stays woody. Price is driven by brand and storage more than by raw age, and heavily wet-stored stock, sold cheaply, is the common trap.
description:
Aged shu is ripe pu-erh that has sat for a decade or more after pressing, long enough for every trace of the fermentation pile to leave and for a soft, sweet, old-wood character to settle in. It will never transform the way raw tea does, because the pile already did the transforming, but a good old ripe is a different and calmer thing from a young one, and it is the cheapest way to drink genuinely old pu-erh.

Nothing is done to it but storage. In Hong Kong and Guangdong warehouses the humidity adds a camphor and herbal aroma and a very soft texture; in Kunming the same tea stays woodier and cleaner. Loose ripe tea aged in the back rooms of Cantonese restaurants is a tradition of its own, served by the pot with dim sum.

In the cup, aged shu is smooth and quiet: dates, old wood, a creamy texture like rice soup, light camphor, sometimes a ginseng-like herbal note, and no earthiness at all. It wants boiling water, two rinses, a clay pot and long steeps, and it gives a long, even session that ends well in a simmering pot. It is the gentlest tea in this group on the stomach.

It is sold by production year, factory and storage, with the Menghai and Kunming factory classics from the late 1990s and 2000s the usual buys and anything from the 1980s a specialist purchase. The storage is the thing to interrogate: a faint cellar note that clears after the rinse is normal for humid-stored tea, a sharp mustiness or a dull, lifeless cup means it was kept too wet. Old ripe is not usually faked by relabelling in the way old raw is, simply because it is worth less, but 'thirty-year-old' loose shu at a market stall is a story, not a date.

For a comfortable evening tea with real age at a sane price, a fifteen-year-old factory ripe cake from clean Guangdong storage is hard to beat.
history:
Aged shu is a description rather than a named tea: ripe pu-erh that has simply been kept for a long time after pressing. It can only be as old as wet-piling itself, which makes it a younger idea than aged raw pu-erh.

Little is documented about how it became something people seek out. Most of what circulates is trade knowledge about factories, storage cities and restaurant stocks, and the age claimed for any given tea is often hard to confirm.
